title: Indian Student Enrollment in US Falls 6.9% as Four-Year Visa Cap and Tighter Scrutiny Take Hold
excerpt: A new DHS rule ending decades-old 'duration of status' for student visas compounds a sharp enrollment decline, with 63% of US institutions expecting further drops in 2026-27.
body:
• Indian student enrollment in the US fell 6.9% in one year — from 378,787 in February 2025 to 352,644 in February 2026 — the sharpest annual drop in over a decade, per Indian Parliament data.
  • A DHS final rule effective September 15, 2026, caps F-1 and J-1 visas at four years, replacing the decades-old "duration of status" framework that let students stay as long as their programs required.
  • The IIE Spring 2026 Snapshot found 63% of 585 US institutions expect international enrollment to decline in 2026-27, with India showing the most pronounced drop in applications.
  • F-1 visa issuances to Indian students fell over 60% last summer, with American consulates in India issuing visas to only about 22,000 students.

A Decade-Low for Indian Students

The number of Indian students enrolled at US institutions has dropped to 352,644 as of February 2026, down from 378,787 a year earlier — a 6.9% decline that marks the sharpest year-on-year fall in over a decade. The figures, drawn from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's SEVIS database, were confirmed by India's Ministry of External Affairs in a written reply to the Rajya Sabha on April 2, 2026.

The decline spans all program levels, from undergraduate to doctoral studies. India remains the largest source country of international students in the US, but the gap with second-ranked China has narrowed for the first time since 2019, according to Collegedunia's analysis of the Parliament data.

Four-Year Visa Cap Replaces Open-Ended Stays

On July 16, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security published a final rule that ends the "duration of status" framework governing student visas since 1978. Effective September 15, 2026, F-1 student visas and J-1 exchange visitor visas will be capped at four years, regardless of program length.

Students needing additional time must apply for extensions directly through USCIS, undergoing biometric vetting, background checks, and fraud screening. The rule also cuts the post-graduation grace period from 60 to 30 days and bars graduate students from changing their educational objectives or transferring institutions without federal authorization.

"International students, many of whom will have spent years in the USA, will now have just 30 days to find an employer to sponsor them or immediately be turned into illegal immigrants. Have these people no understanding of how life works?"

— David J. Bier, Immigration Studies Director, Cato Institute

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the changes, saying in a statement that "the outdated 'duration of status' system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud." Current visa holders already in the US will automatically transition to the new framework, with their stays capped at four years from the rule's effective date.

Universities Brace for Further Declines

The enrollment slide is not limited to Indian students. The Institute of International Education's 2026 Spring Snapshot, surveying 585 US colleges and universities, found that 63% expect international student numbers to fall in the 2026-27 academic year. Only 11% forecast an increase. Among applications, 59% of institutions reported a decrease in volumes, with India showing the most pronounced drops — only 39% of institutions reported stable or increased Indian applications.

The contributing factors are compounding. Nearly all respondents (92%) cited visa processing issues — delays in scheduling and rising rejection rates — as the most significant factor, according to IIE. Eighty percent pointed to the expanded travel ban, and 77% cited increased competition from universities in Canada, the UK, and Australia drawing students away from the US.

Visa Bottlenecks Hit India Hardest

The pipeline problems began well before the new four-year cap rule. F-1 visa issuances to Indian students dropped over 60% last summer, with American consulates in India issuing visas to roughly 22,000 students — a fraction of prior years, according to a Chronicle of Higher Education analysis of State Department data. Nationally, new international student arrivals fell 19% year-over-year, with Indian arrivals down 44.5% — a shortfall of over 33,000 students, according to Inside Higher Ed.

Visa wait times remain a barrier. As of February 2026, student visa appointment waits ranged from two months in Kolkata to 2.5 months in Mumbai and Hyderabad, according to State Department data.

Financial and Strategic Fallout

The enrollment decline carries significant financial consequences for US universities that depend heavily on international tuition revenue. The University of North Texas, which hosts roughly 11,900 international students, reported losing an estimated $47.3 million in anticipated tuition revenue from slowing enrollment. Central Michigan University expects a 23% drop in nondomestic students this year. Indiana University Indianapolis reported 26% fewer international students.

For Indian families weighing a US education, the calculus has shifted. Shorter visa windows, costlier extensions, and uncertain post-graduation pathways are steering more students toward Canada, the UK, and Australia — destinations actively courting the same talent pool the US is making harder to retain.
